subChunks.title: Service Records, Medal Rolls & Pension Files
subChunks.hookHtml: A British soldier's service record can be more biographically detailed than any civil registration document — listing birthplace, physical description, religion, next of kin, wounds received, and conduct across twenty years of service. For millions of families, the military records of a grandfather or great-grandfather are the single richest genealogical source that exists for that generation. Learning to navigate them is one of the most rewarding skills a genealogist can acquire.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Overview of British military record categories

British military records divide broadly into:

  • Service records — documenting an individual soldier's career (enlistment, ranks, postings, conduct, discharge)
  • Medal rolls — listing individuals who received specific campaign or gallantry medals
  • Pension records — Chelsea Royal Hospital (army) and Greenwich Hospital (navy) pension files, often extraordinarily detailed
  • Muster rolls — periodic lists of a regiment's serving members
  • War diaries — unit-level operational records kept daily, especially from WW1 onward

Army service records — the Burnt Documents problem

The single most important fact about British Army WW1 service records is the Burnt Documents. In September 1940, a German bombing raid on Arnside Street in London destroyed roughly 60% of Army service records for soldiers who served in WW1. What survived — known as the "Burnt Documents" — was water-damaged as well as fire-damaged; the surviving records are on Ancestry and have partial survival rates varying by regiment. If your ancestor's WW1 service record is missing, it was probably destroyed in 1940, not misfiled.

Substitutes for missing WW1 service records:

  • Medal Index Cards (MIC) — cards issued for every man awarded the 1914 Star, 1914–15 Star, British War Medal, or Victory Medal. Searchable on Ancestry and TNA. Gives service number, rank, regiment, and medal entitlement — and sometimes theatre of war and entry date.
  • Pension records (WO364) — service records created for pension purposes, held at TNA. Survived the 1940 bombing better than regular service records.
  • Regimental histories and war diaries — unit-level records that place a soldier in a specific engagement even when the personal record is lost.
  • Silver War Badge rolls — issued to men discharged due to wounds or sickness, 1916–1920.

Army service records — pre-WW1

For soldiers who served before WW1, the records landscape is different and generally better preserved:

  • WO97 (1756–1913): Soldiers' Documents — discharge papers filed at Chelsea Hospital. These are the most genealogically rich pre-WW1 army record: they give birth year and parish, physical description (height, hair, eye colour, marks), trade before enlistment, conduct record, wounds or disabilities, and sometimes next of kin. Fully indexed and available on Ancestry and FindMyPast.
  • Muster rolls (WO10–16): periodic lists of every man in a regiment, going back to the 18th century. Less personal detail than WO97 but establish presence in a unit at a given date.
  • Description books: physical descriptions of soldiers kept at regimental level — often the only record with a soldier's birthplace when no discharge document survives.

Royal Navy records

Navy records are organised differently from Army records. Key series:

  • Continuous Service Engagement Books (ADM139/196): from 1853, when continuous (as opposed to voyage-by-voyage) naval service was introduced. Gives birthplace, physical description, and service history.
  • Muster books (ADM36/37/38/41): list of every man aboard a named ship for a specified period. From the 18th century. Useful to establish that a sailor served on a named vessel.
  • Pension records (PMG): Greenwich Hospital pensions — extraordinarily detailed, often giving the sailor's full biography.

Commonwealth war graves

For all Commonwealth soldiers who died in WW1 or WW2, the Commonwealth War Graves Commission (CWGC) maintains a free online database at cwgc.org. Each entry gives name, rank, regiment, date of death, age (if known), and grave or memorial location. The CWGC database is a starting point for any search — if your ancestor died in service, this will confirm it and give the regiment.

Campaign medals — reading the entitlement

British campaign medals were awarded by entitlement (not discretion), so medal rolls are nearly complete lists of participants in a campaign. Key WW1 medal groups:

  • 1914 Star: served in France/Belgium before 22 November 1914
  • 1914–15 Star: served in any theatre 1914–31 December 1915
  • British War Medal: served anywhere 1914–20
  • Victory Medal: served in an operational theatre 1914–18

A man holding all four is called a "Mons Star" holder — one of the original BEF who saw action at Mons in August 1914. This immediately tells you his regiment was part of the British Expeditionary Force in the opening weeks of WW1.

storyBeats.text: Theodora opens a folder stamped 'WO97' along the spine. Inside is a discharge document — its edges charred brown, its handwriting smudged but readable. She holds it carefully in both hands.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: A soldier's discharge paper from the 1880s. Look what it gives us: his name, his regiment, the date and parish of his birth, his trade before enlistment — shoemaker — his height and the colour of his hair, the marks on his body, his conduct record over fifteen years. His wife's name — she had to be registered as next of kin to receive a widow's pension if he died in service. This is a biography. No civil registration document will ever tell you this much about a labouring man.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: But for the Great War — the First World War — you must know the disaster. In September 1940, German bombs hit a storage building in London. They destroyed roughly sixty percent of the service records for British soldiers of 1914 to 1918. What survived was then soaked by the firefighters' hoses. We call what remains the Burnt Documents. If you cannot find your great-grandfather's WW1 service record, it is almost certainly because it burned in 1940, not because it never existed.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: But do not give up. The Medal Index Cards survived. Every man who qualified for the 1914 Star, the British War Medal, or the Victory Medal has an index card — and those cards give regiment, service number, and often the theatre of war. The pension records often survived too. And the Commonwealth War Graves Commission has every man who died in service — free, online, complete. Begin there. Find his regiment. Then find the regiment's war diary. One entry per day, recording where the unit was and what it did. Your ancestor's name may never appear in the diary — they were private soldiers, not officers. But you will know exactly where he was on any given date, and that is something.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Anchor military record types

Retrieve from memory:

  • What are the Burnt Documents and when was the disaster?
  • Name two substitutes for a missing WW1 service record.
  • What series reference covers pre-WW1 Army discharge papers at TNA (the most genealogically rich series)?
  • What does the CWGC database provide, and how do you access it?
  • What does it mean if an ancestor held the 1914 Star?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
The Burnt Documents are the British Army WW1 service records partially destroyed when German bombs hit a London storage building in September 1940, destroying approximately 60% of records; the surviving papers were also water-damaged by firefighters.

Two substitutes for a missing WW1 service record: (1) Medal Index Cards (MIC) — cards issued for every man awarded the main WW1 campaign medals, giving regiment, service number, and medal entitlement; (2) Pension records (WO364) — created for pension purposes and surviving the 1940 bombing better than regular service records.

The WO97 series (Soldiers' Documents, 1756–1913) at TNA covers pre-WW1 army discharge papers. These give birth year and parish, physical description, trade before enlistment, conduct record, wounds or disabilities, and sometimes next of kin.

The Commonwealth War Graves Commission (CWGC) database at cwgc.org provides the name, rank, regiment, date of death, age, and grave or memorial location for every Commonwealth soldier who died in WW1 or WW2. It is free to search online.

The 1914 Star was awarded to men who served in France or Belgium before 22 November 1914 — meaning the holder was part of the original British Expeditionary Force (BEF) and saw action in the opening weeks of WW1, including the retreat from Mons.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Tracing a WW1 ancestor with missing service record

Your great-grandfather William Murphy is believed to have served in the British Army in WW1. His service record cannot be found on Ancestry or FindMyPast. Family tradition says he was gassed on the Western Front and returned with lung damage, dying of chest problems in 1931. You know only his name, approximate birth year (c.1890), and that he lived in Manchester before the war.

Write a research plan (350–450 words) detailing: (1) which alternative records you would search and why; (2) what information you hope to derive from each; (3) how you would identify his regiment if none of the records give it directly; (4) what the Manchester connection might help you find.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Research plan for William Murphy (b. c.1890, Manchester; WW1 service, service record missing):

The missing service record was almost certainly destroyed in the 1940 Arnside Street bombing. I would search the following alternatives:

1. Medal Index Cards (Ancestry / TNA WO372): Every qualifying WW1 soldier has an MIC. Searching for William Murphy born c.1890 should yield his regiment number and medal entitlement. The MIC may also indicate which theatre he served in (Western Front stars would be consistent with gassing).

2. Pension records (TNA WO364, also on Ancestry): Created for disability and dependant pensions, these survived better than standard service records. Given that William returned with lung damage from gas, he may have been discharged on medical grounds — making a disability pension file likely. These files can be very detailed, including medical examination records describing the nature of his injuries.

3. CWGC database (cwgc.org): William survived the war, so he will not be in CWGC — but I would check to confirm no same-name death matches, and to understand the likely regiments for Manchester men (the Manchester Regiment, Salford Pals, and various Lancashire Fusiliers battalions recruited heavily in the Manchester area).

4. Silver War Badge rolls (TNA WO329): If William was discharged due to wounds or medical discharge 1916–1920, he may appear on the Silver War Badge rolls — giving regiment and service number.

5. Manchester Regiment records: Knowing that Manchester men most likely served in the Manchester Regiment or its affiliated Pals battalions, I would search regimental histories and war diaries (WO95 at TNA, partially on Ancestry) for accounts of gas attacks involving Manchester units — notably the Battle of Loos (1915) and other Western Front engagements where phosgene and chlorine were used.

6. Manchester local records: Manchester local newspapers (digitised on the British Newspaper Archive) published casualty lists, honour rolls, and reports of men returning wounded. A William Murphy 'gassed on the Western Front' might appear in a 1916 or 1917 Manchester Evening News report. Manchester City Archives may hold tribunal records from the Military Service Act 1916 (conscription) if William was called up rather than volunteering.

Expected outcome: The MIC and pension records together should give regiment, service number, approximate discharge date, and medical grounds for discharge — providing enough information to trace the relevant war diary and confirm his Western Front service.

TNA series of pre-WW1 British Army discharge papers (1756–1913), giving birthplace, physical description, trade, conduct, and next of kin — among the richest genealogical records for working-class men.
The organisation maintaining graves and memorials for Commonwealth soldiers killed in WW1 and WW2; free searchable database at cwgc.org gives name, rank, regiment, and burial location.
The collective term for British Army WW1 service records partially destroyed in the September 1940 German bombing of Arnside Street, London — approximately 60% of records were lost.

Daily operational records kept by British Army units from WW1, recording location and activities — held at TNA; most are available via Ancestry and provide context for an ancestor's service even when personal records are missing.

questions.questionHtml: Approximately what percentage of British Army WW1 service records were destroyed in the 1940 Arnside Street bombing?
questions.explanationHtml: The September 1940 bombing and subsequent firefighting destroyed approximately 60% of the British Army service records for WW1 soldiers. The surviving 40% — known as the 'Burnt Documents' — suffered fire and water damage and are available on Ancestry and TNA. This is the single most important fact to know when researching a British WW1 ancestor.

questions.questionHtml: You cannot find a WW1 service record for your ancestor Corporal John Walsh, Royal Fusiliers. What is your best next source?
options: Medal Index Cards (WO372) on Ancestry — these survived separately and will give regiment, service number, and medal entitlement
The 1911 census — it will list him if he was born before 1901
The GRO birth index — to confirm his date of birth before continuing
You cannot research further — without the service record, nothing is recoverable
questions.correctAnswer: Medal Index Cards (WO372) on Ancestry — these survived separately and will give regiment, service number, and medal entitlement
questions.explanationHtml: Medal Index Cards were kept separately from service records and survived the 1940 bombing. Every man who qualified for the main WW1 campaign medals (1914 Star, 1914–15 Star, British War Medal, Victory Medal) has a card giving his regiment, service number, and medal entitlement. The MIC is the essential first substitute when a service record is missing — it provides enough information to then search pension records (WO364), regimental histories, and war diaries.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher finds that their ancestor holds both the 1914 Star and the British War Medal but NOT the Victory Medal. What does this combination suggest about his service?
options: He served in France or Belgium before November 1914 (earning the 1914 Star) and served through 1914–18 generally (British War Medal), but may not have survived to the end of the war or may have been discharged before qualifying for the Victory Medal — the missing Victory Medal is the anomaly to investigate
This combination proves he served in Gallipoli rather than the Western Front
The 1914 Star and British War Medal are the same medal issued under two names
Holding both medals means he served in the Royal Navy rather than the Army
questions.correctAnswer: He served in France or Belgium before November 1914 (earning the 1914 Star) and served through 1914–18 generally (British War Medal), but may not have survived to the end of the war or may have been discharged before qualifying for the Victory Medal — the missing Victory Medal is the anomaly to investigate
questions.explanationHtml: The Victory Medal was awarded to those who served in an operational theatre in WW1 — almost everyone who earned the British War Medal also earned the Victory Medal. Missing the Victory Medal while holding the 1914 Star and British War Medal is unusual and suggests either death in service before the medals were gazetted, a discharge under unusual circumstances, or a clerical omission. The CWGC database would confirm whether he died in service. Pension records would indicate an early medical discharge. The missing medal is a research clue, not an administrative error to be ignored.
